summary.text: Principal component analysis is a linear technique that transforms data so the directions capturing the largest variation can be easily identified.
The first principal component explains the most variance, and each next one explains the most of what is left once earlier ones are removed.
The components are eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, so they are computed by eigendecomposition or singular value decomposition.

facts.label: Inventor
facts.value: Karl Pearson in 1901; Hotelling developed and named it in the 1930s

facts.label: Best used when
facts.value: Many variables are highly correlated with each other

facts.label: Where it appears
facts.value: Population genetics, microbiome studies and atmospheric science

facts.label: Variance share
facts.value: An eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues

facts.label: Plotting habit
facts.value: The first two components often plot data in two dimensions

items.prompt: A spreadsheet has dozens of columns that mostly rise and fall together. Is principal component analysis a good fit?

options.label: No, it needs columns that are unrelated
No, it only works on two columns
Yes, it suits many highly correlated variables
Yes, but only if the columns are identical

items.explain: It is most commonly used when many variables are highly correlated and one wants fewer, independent ones.

items.prompt: Which direction does the first principal component point along?

options.label: The one where the projected data varies the most
The one where the projected data varies the least
The one along the first column of the data
The one that follows the average value

items.explain: The first component is the direction that maximizes the variance of the projected data.

items.prompt: The principal components are eigenvectors of which matrix built from the data?

options.label: The matrix of raw measurements
The covariance matrix
The identity matrix
The matrix of averages

items.explain: For either way of defining them, the components are eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix.

items.prompt: A covariance matrix has eigenvalues 6, 3 and 1. What share of the total variance belongs to the eigenvector with eigenvalue 6?

options.label: 30 percent
6 percent
150 percent
60 percent

items.explain: Divide that eigenvalue by the sum of all eigenvalues: 6 out of 10.

items.prompt: A biologist has dozens of measurements per sample and wants a flat picture where related samples sit together. What helps?

options.label: Plot the data on the first two principal components
Plot only the last principal component
Plot every variable against every other
Delete the samples that look different

items.explain: Plotting the first two principal components lets one visually identify clusters of closely related points.

items.prompt: Before looking for the axes, what must be done to each variable in the data?

options.label: Square every value
Sort the values from small to large
Rescale all values to the range of zero to one
Subtract its mean so it is centered on zero

items.explain: Each variable is centered on 0 by subtracting the mean of its observed values.
